Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones
A specific texture associated with the event

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I have to be on guard all the time
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: For a 55-year-old female bank teller with combat trauma, 'Bicycle' as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items imply interpersonal/loss and sensory trauma reminders, while bicycle is a highly specific cue with no support from threat, memory, or appraisal content and no clear combat linkage. This makes it clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'You can never know who will harm you' is too nonspecific relative to the rest of the profile. The threat items emphasize overt vigilance and reading faces/body language, and the appraisals also center betrayal and loss of meaning. This item implies diffuse interpersonal mistrust without a corresponding interpersonal memory or trigger pattern beyond betrayal, making the negative appraisal set less coherent with the otherwise combat/loss-focused formulation.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise organized around combat-linked threat, sensory triggers, and disjointed trauma memory, but the betrayal appraisal introduces a different interpersonal trauma theme that is not supported by the other selected items. With combat trauma, betrayal can occur, but here there are no corresponding triggers, memory content, or threat/appraisal items suggesting moral injury, friendly-fire, command betrayal, or interpersonal violation. This makes the betrayal item the main clinically incoherent element relative to the rest of the profile and formulation.

vignette:
María was fifty-five years old, a divorced bank teller who had spent most of her adult life in a small city in the Midwest, a long way from the rural village in El Salvador where she had grown up. The event that had reshaped her world had happened decades ago, during the civil war, when she was a young woman. She had been walking with her cousin to a nearby market when a mortar shell landed in the road ahead of them. The explosion was a single, deafening crack that seemed to tear the air itself, followed by a ringing silence and the sudden, peculiar texture of dust and grit settling on her skin. Her cousin, who had been a step ahead of her, was killed instantly. María had not been physically harmed, but the image of her cousin’s body, the sound of the blast, and the feeling of that fine, chalky dust on her hands had never left her. She had come to the United States soon after, married, had a child, and divorced, building a life that seemed stable, but the memory of that day felt fragmented, almost unreal. When she tried to explain it to her therapist, she would lose the thread, unable to put the sequence of events in the right order, and the story would end with her shaking her head, saying, “It’s too much. It can’t have been real.”

Years passed, and the memory stayed buried, but the texture of it had begun to surface in her daily life. She worked behind a counter, handling cash and greeting customers, but she found herself constantly scanning her surroundings for signs of danger, studying the faces and body language of everyone who approached her window. She had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, and that she had to be on guard all the time. This belief was reinforced by a powerful physical reactivity that she could not control. A customer would inadvertently tap the countertop with their fingernail, and the sharp, percussive sound would trigger a full-body startle, her heart pounding, her hands trembling. The sound of a car backfiring outside the bank would send her ducking behind the counter, her mind reeling with the old explosion, the dust, the silence. These triggers—the bang, the texture of a rough paper, even a casual conversation about someone losing a loved one—would pull her back into the confused, unreal memory, and the memory itself would then make her feel even more unsafe, as if the danger were present, right here, in the bank lobby.

The loop tightened over the months. The more the memory intruded, the more she scanned for threats, and the more she scanned, the more she felt the world was dangerous, which in turn made the smallest sound a potential explosion. She had lost any sense of meaning in her life; her work felt hollow, her relationships distant. She had stopped going to her son’s house for dinner because his dog, a friendly golden retriever, had a rough, dusty coat that reminded her of the grit on her hands after the blast. She did not explain this to anyone. It seemed too absurd, too fragile. What finally brought her to seek help was a panic attack in the bank’s break room after a co-worker accidentally dropped a metal tray. She had been found on the floor, sobbing, unable to speak. She was terrified that she was losing her mind, but she was also, quietly, hoping that someone could make the world feel safe again, or at least show her how to stop seeing the explosion in every sudden sound.
